name: mtls
context: A system whose services, devices, or partners call each other across a network that nobody owns end to end. Traditional deployment treats 'inside the perimeter' as proof of identity, so a compromised pod, a flat cluster network, or a partner on the same VLAN inherits the trust of everything behind the firewall. Mutual TLS replaces location with a cryptographic claim: in the TLS 1.3 handshake the server sends a CertificateRequest and the client answers with its own certificate and a CertificateVerify proof of possession, so both endpoints are authenticated before any application byte moves. The pattern is architectural, not a library call, because it forces structural decisions - who runs the CA, where TLS terminates (application, sidecar, or gateway), what the identity claim looks like, and how certificates reach workloads that are created and destroyed continuously.
benefits: Network location stops being a credential: authorization binds to a verified identity claim rather than to a subnet, which is what makes the zero-trust PDP/PEP model enforceable at all

Short-lived credentials replace revocation. SPIFFE recommends lifetimes as short as one hour; a leaked certificate expires before an attacker can use it, so CRLs and OCSP round trips become optional rather than mandatory
Per-service identities remove the shared internal credential. One leaked service key no longer opens every service on the internal network
A sidecar proxy (Envoy, linkerd2-proxy) can originate and terminate mTLS so application code never touches a key, a CA, or a rotation timer
Identity attestation removes the pre-shared-secret bootstrap problem: SPIRE proves which host and which process a workload is before issuing an SVID

The verified identity is bindable into a stronger token. RFC 8705 certificate-bound access tokens carry the client certificate hash in a `cnf` claim, so a stolen bearer token is useless to a party without that specific certificate
tradeoffs: The certificate lifecycle is an operational burden that scales badly by hand. Two services with a hand-run CA is an afternoon; twenty services with hourly rotation is a standing job of issuance, distribution, renewal and revocation

Revocation is genuinely hard: CRLs grow into megabytes, OCSP adds a round trip to every handshake, and stapling is not universally supported. Short TTL is the pragmatic substitute, and it trades fast compromise response for bounded exposure
Protection is per hop, not end to end. Any hop that terminates TLS holds plaintext, so an L7 proxy that re-encrypts to the next service moves the trust boundary rather than removing it
L7 load balancers routinely strip client certificates; the deployment must use TCP passthrough or re-encrypt, and that decision changes the topology
Extension Key Usage errors are silent until a handshake fails. A 'server' template issued to a client lacks clientAuth (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2) and some TLS stacks reject it without saying why
Handshake and encryption cost is real at high connection rates; TLS 1.3 at 1-RTT helps, but the first connection on every certificate lifetime pays full price

Cross-cluster trust does not come free. Cilium documents that there is no option to build a single trust domain spanning multiple clusters, so a Cluster Mesh and an mTLS deployment can be mutually exclusive
use_cases: Service-to-service calls inside a Kubernetes cluster where any pod may be hostile
A gateway authenticating a fleet of field devices that come and go without a provisioning step
Partner and B2B integrations where neither side controls the other's network
Splitting trust domains so a payment namespace cannot present a valid identity to the ordering namespace
avoid_when: All calls stay inside one process or one host - there is no network hop to authenticate
The estate is a handful of services with no platform to run a control plane; hand-managed mTLS costs more than the threat it removes
The requirement is end-to-end confidentiality against the terminating proxies, which per-hop transport encryption cannot deliver
The platform has no attestation story, so certificates would have to be injected as static files - that reintroduces the secret in the image
component_types: SPIRE server (root of trust for the trust domain)
technology_stack: SPIFFE / SPIRE (X.509-SVID, Workload API over Unix domain socket)
anti_patterns: Year-long certificates. A long-lived certificate is a long-lived secret; the mTLS benefit collapses the moment it is stolen
Leaving PeerAuthentication in PERMISSIVE mode after migration because plaintext callers still exist. Production ends at STRICT
Conflating authentication with authorization: mTLS proves who called, it does not decide whether that caller may perform the operation
Trusting any certificate chaining to the internal CA without a SAN policy, which makes the identity claim meaningless and reduces mTLS to encryption
Trust bundles that omit intermediate CAs, surfacing as `unknown CA` on one side of a connection while the other side looks healthy
Rotating manually or on a schedule that can slip. The first missed renewal presents as handshake failures that read like a network fault
Handing the certificate to the application as a mounted file, so it is copied into logs, images, and crash dumps
design_principles: Never infer trust from network position; every request carries a verified identity claim
Make credentials short-lived so that revocation becomes unnecessary rather than merely difficult
Bind identity, not location: the SAN holds the identity the policy engine matches, not the address the packet came from
Bootstrap identity from platform attestation instead of a pre-shared secret, so no workload has to be born holding a credential
Keep authentication and authorization as separate decisions with separate components
Prefer cryptographic agility: the identity format should be portable across runtimes
best_practices: Issue per-workload certificates with a SPIFFE ID URI in the SAN (spiffe://trust.domain/path), not a shared service wildcard
Keep TLS termination in a sidecar that receives certs via the SDS API, keeping private keys in tmpfs and off disk
Authenticate peer sessions once per certificate lifetime and cache the result in the datapath, rather than handshaking per connection - the model Cilium's auth map implements
Use PERMISSIVE only as a migration step, and track it as a removal ticket rather than as a steady state
Give server certs serverAuth EKU and client certs clientAuth EKU; validate both ends of the chain and ship the full chain from the peer
Verify SAN, EKU, validity and chain on every handshake; a certificate that parses is not a certificate that is acceptable
If identity also needs to drive API access, bind the token to the certificate per RFC 8705 so a stolen token cannot be replayed by another holder
references: Cilium CFP-22215, Mutual Authentication for Service Mesh - https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/blob/main/cilium/CFP-22215-mutual-auth-for-service-mesh.md
OWASP ASVS 5.0, V12 Secure Communication (12.3.5 requires strong authentication for intra-service communication) - https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x21-V12-Secure-Communication.md
Curity, Harden OAuth Client Credentials with SPIFFE X509 SVIDs (RFC 8705 certificate-bound tokens) - https://curity.io/resources/learn/oauth-client-credentials-spiffe-x509-svids/
